questions.question: Define web clients and web servers with examples.
questions.answer:
Web Client:
A web client is a software application or device that requests resources/services from a web server over the internet using HTTP/HTTPS protocols.
- Examples: Web browsers (Google Chrome, Mozilla Firefox, Microsoft Edge), mobile apps that fetch data from APIs.
- Role: Sends HTTP requests and renders the received HTML, CSS, JavaScript responses.

Web Server:
A web server is software or hardware that stores, processes, and serves web content (HTML pages, images, files) to clients in response to their requests.
- Examples: Apache HTTP Server, Nginx, Microsoft IIS, Node.js (with Express).
- Role: Listens on port 80 (HTTP) or 443 (HTTPS), processes incoming requests, and sends appropriate responses.

Interaction:
1. Client (browser) sends HTTP GET request to server.
2. Server locates the resource and sends HTTP response (200 OK with HTML content).
3. Browser renders the received content for the user.

Describe the rules for creating XML document. Create a XML file with simple type and elements with attribute and nested elements. Write its equivalent XSD.
questions.answer:
Rules for Creating XML Documents:
1. Every XML document must have a single root element.
2. All elements must be properly closed (e.g., <name></name> or <name/>).
3. XML tags are case-sensitive (<Name> and <name> are different).
4. Elements must be properly nested (no overlapping tags).
5. Attribute values must be quoted (single or double).
6. XML declaration is recommended: <?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
7. Special characters must use entities: & < > ' "

Describe client server architecture with its types.
questions.answer:
Client-Server Architecture:
A client-server architecture is a computing model where client machines request services/resources from a centralized server over a network.

Components:
- Client: Requests resources or services. Examples: browsers, desktop apps.
- Server: Provides resources, processes requests, and sends responses. Examples: Apache, Nginx, MySQL.

Types:
1. One-Tier Architecture: All components (UI, logic, database) are on a single machine. Example: Standalone desktop application.

2. Two-Tier Architecture: Client communicates directly with the database server. Example: Desktop app directly querying MySQL on a server.

3. Three-Tier Architecture: Consists of Presentation Layer (client), Business Logic Layer (application server), and Data Layer (database server). Example: Web applications using PHP/Node.js with MySQL.

4. N-Tier Architecture: Extension of three-tier with multiple layers for security, caching, load balancing, etc. Used in large enterprise applications.

Advantages: Centralized data management, scalability, easy maintenance, security control.

Describe the WWW, web client and web server.
questions.answer:
WWW (World Wide Web):
The World Wide Web is a system of interlinked hypertext documents accessed via the Internet using a web browser. It was invented by Tim Berners-Lee in 1989. Key technologies: HTTP/HTTPS protocol, HTML for content, URLs for addressing, and browsers for accessing content.

Web Client:
A web client is any program or device that requests and receives content from a web server.
- Examples: Chrome, Firefox, Edge, mobile browsers, REST API clients.
- The client sends an HTTP request (GET/POST) and processes the response (HTML, JSON, etc.).

Web Server:
A web server is software (or hardware) that handles incoming HTTP requests from clients and returns appropriate responses.
- Examples: Apache, Nginx, IIS.
- Functions: Hosting websites, serving static/dynamic pages, handling CGI scripts, SSL termination.

Interaction Flow:
1. User types URL in browser (client).
2. DNS resolves the domain to an IP address.
3. Client sends HTTP GET request to server.
4. Server processes the request and returns HTTP response (HTML, images, etc.).
5. Browser renders the content for the user.

questions.question: What is XML? Why is it called extensible? Mention the use of XML.
questions.answer:
XML (eXtensible Markup Language): XML is a markup language designed to store, transport, and structure data in a human-readable and machine-readable format. It was developed by the W3C. Why is it called Extensible? XML is called extensible because: - Unlike HTML (which has fixed predefined tags like

,

), XML allows users to define their own custom tags. - Users can extend XML to fit their specific needs — for example, , , can all be valid XML tags. - New tags can be added without breaking existing applications. Uses of XML: 1. Data storage and transportation between applications. 2. Web services (SOAP uses XML for messaging). 3. Configuration files (Maven pom.xml, Android AndroidManifest.xml). 4. RSS/Atom feeds for news syndication. 5. Microsoft Office documents (.docx, .xlsx are actually XML inside ZIP). 6. Database data exchange between different systems. 7. SVG (Scalable Vector Graphics) is XML-based.

questions.answer:
Use of XML: (See web-22 answer for uses)
XML is used to store, transport, and structure data in a platform-independent format useful for data exchange, configuration, and web services.

XML File with Simple and Complex Types (bookstore.xml):
```xml
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<!DOCTYPE bookstore SYSTEM "bookstore.dtd">
<bookstore>
  <book category="fiction">
    <title>Harry Potter</title>
    <author>J.K. Rowling</author>
    <price>29.99</price>
    <year>1997</year>
  </book>
  <book category="education">
    <title>Web Technology</title>
    <author>Adesh Pandey</author>
    <price>15.50</price>
    <year>2018</year>
  </book>
</bookstore>
```
Simple type elements: title, author, price, year (contain only text content).
Complex type elements: bookstore, book (contain child elements or attributes).

DTD File (bookstore.dtd):
```dtd
<!ELEMENT bookstore (book+)>
<!ELEMENT book (title, author, price, year)>
<!ATTLIST book category CDATA #REQUIRED>
<!ELEMENT title (#PCDATA)>
<!ELEMENT author (#PCDATA)>
<!ELEMENT price (#PCDATA)>
<!ELEMENT year (#PCDATA)>
```
Explanation:
- ELEMENT declares the element and its content model.
- book+ means one or more book elements.
- #PCDATA means parsed character data (text).
- ATTLIST declares attributes; CDATA means character data; #REQUIRED means mandatory.

Differentiate Web 1.0 from Web 2.0.
questions.answer:
Web 1.0 vs Web 2.0:

| Feature         | Web 1.0                            | Web 2.0                                |
|-----------------|------------------------------------|----------------------------------------|
| Era             | 1991-2004                          | 2004-present                           |
| Nature          | Read-only (static)                 | Read-write (dynamic and interactive)   |
| Content         | Created only by website owners     | Created by users (user-generated)      |
| Technology      | HTML, CSS (basic)                  | HTML5, CSS3, JavaScript, AJAX, APIs    |
| Interaction     | Passive browsing                   | Active participation and collaboration |
| Examples        | Personal homepages, early portals  | Facebook, YouTube, Wikipedia, Twitter  |
| Data sharing    | Limited, no sharing                | Social sharing, collaboration tools    |
| Web pages       | Flat HTML files                    | Dynamic apps, web services             |
| Personalization | None                               | Personalized feeds, recommendations    |

Summary: Web 1.0 was a one-way information delivery system. Web 2.0 transformed the web into a participative social platform where users create, share, and collaborate on content.

What is XML Namespace? How it is used to avoid element name conflict in XML? Justify with an example.
questions.answer:
XML Namespace:
An XML Namespace is a mechanism to avoid element name conflicts when XML documents from different vocabularies are combined. It associates element/attribute names with a URI (Uniform Resource Identifier) to make them globally unique.

Problem without Namespaces:
If two XML vocabularies both define a <table> element, combining them causes ambiguity — is <table> a furniture table or an HTML table?

Syntax: xmlns:prefix="URI"
- xmlns: declares a namespace.
- prefix: A short alias used before element names.
- URI: A unique identifier (often a URL, but doesn't need to resolve to anything).

Example with conflict and solution:
```xml
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<root
  xmlns:html="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
  xmlns:furniture="http://www.furniture.com/schema">

  <!-- HTML table element -->
  <html:table>
    <html:tr>
      <html:td>Row 1, Cell 1</html:td>
    </html:tr>
  </html:table>

  <!-- Furniture table element -->
  <furniture:table>
    <furniture:material>Wood</furniture:material>
    <furniture:legs>4</furniture:legs>
  </furniture:table>

</root>
```
Now html:table and furniture:table are clearly different — no conflict. The URI is just a unique identifier, not necessarily a real website.

questions.question: Discuss about different JSON data types.
questions.answer:
JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) Data Types:
JSON is a lightweight, text-based data interchange format. It supports the following data types:

1. String: Text enclosed in double quotes.
   Example: "name": "Ram Sharma"

2. Number: Integer or floating-point numbers (no quotes).
   Example: "age": 21, "gpa": 3.75

3. Boolean: true or false (lowercase).
   Example: "isStudent": true, "isGraduated": false

4. Null: Represents an empty or unknown value.
   Example: "middleName": null

5. Array: An ordered list of values enclosed in square brackets.
   Example: "subjects": ["Web Tech", "Crypto", "Simulation"]

6. Object: An unordered collection of key-value pairs enclosed in curly braces.
   Example: "address": {"city": "Kathmandu", "country": "Nepal"}

Full Example:
```json
{
  "id": 101,
  "name": "Ram Sharma",
  "gpa": 3.8,
  "isActive": true,
  "middleName": null,
  "subjects": ["Web Tech", "Cryptography"],
  "address": {
    "city": "Kathmandu",
    "zip": "44600"
  }
}
```
Note: JSON keys must always be strings (double-quoted). JSON does NOT support comments, undefined, or functions.

questions.question: What is DTD? Create an XML file and write its equivalent DTD.
questions.answer:
DTD (Document Type Definition):
A DTD defines the legal structure of an XML document — which elements are allowed, their order, how many times they can appear, and what attributes they can have. DTD can be internal (inside the XML) or external (separate .dtd file).

DTD Declaration types:
- <!ELEMENT>: Declares an element and its content model.
- <!ATTLIST>: Declares attributes for elements.
- <!ENTITY>: Declares entity shortcuts.
- Content models: (#PCDATA) = text, (child1, child2) = sequence, (a|b) = choice, + = one or more, * = zero or more, ? = optional.

XML File (college.xml):
```xml
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<!DOCTYPE college SYSTEM "college.dtd">
<college>
  <department name="CSIT">
    <student>

Write the structure of XML file with example. Write XML and DTD to describe 'weather report' as an element and 'date, location, city, state and temperature range' as its attributes.
questions.answer:
Structure of XML File:
An XML file has the following structure:
1. XML Declaration: <?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
2. DOCTYPE declaration (optional, for DTD reference).
3. Root element (exactly one).
4. Child elements nested inside the root.
5. Attributes within element opening tags.
6. Text content inside elements.
7. Comments: <!-- comment -->
8. Closing tags matching every opening tag.

XML File (weather.xml) with 'weather_report' element and attributes:
```xml
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<!DOCTYPE weather_report SYSTEM "weather.dtd">
<weather_report
  date="2082-01-15"
  location="South Asia"
  city="Kathmandu"
  state="Bagmati"
  temperature_range="15-25C">
  <description>Partly cloudy with mild temperatures expected throughout the day.</description>
  <humidity>65%</humidity>
  <wind_speed>12 km/h</wind_speed>
</weather_report>
```

DTD File (weather.dtd):
```dtd
<!ELEMENT weather_report (description, humidity, wind_speed)>
<!ATTLIST weather_report
  date             CDATA #REQUIRED
  location         CDATA #REQUIRED
  city             CDATA #REQUIRED
  state            CDATA #REQUIRED
  temperature_range CDATA #REQUIRED
>
<!ELEMENT description (#PCDATA)>
<!ELEMENT humidity (#PCDATA)>
<!ELEMENT wind_speed (#PCDATA)>
```
Explanation: All five properties (date, location, city, state, temperature_range) are defined as CDATA (character data) attributes of weather_report and are all REQUIRED.

Difference between Static and Dynamic website.
questions.answer:
Static vs Dynamic Website:

| Feature           | Static Website                        | Dynamic Website                           |
|-------------------|---------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------|
| Content           | Fixed, same for all users             | Changes based on user/time/database       |
| Technology        | HTML, CSS only                        | HTML, CSS, JavaScript, PHP, databases     |
| Server-side code  | No server-side processing             | Server-side scripting (PHP, Node.js, etc) |
| Database          | Not required                          | Required (MySQL, MongoDB, etc.)           |
| Interactivity     | No user interaction                   | Highly interactive, user-driven           |
| Update method     | Developer manually edits HTML files   | CMS or backend updates database           |
| Loading speed     | Very fast                             | Slightly slower (server processing)       |
| Cost              | Low (simple hosting)                  | Higher (server + database)                |
| Examples          | Personal portfolios, brochure sites   | E-commerce, social media, web apps        |
| Maintenance       | Requires technical knowledge to update| Non-technical users can update via CMS    |

Summary: Static websites display the same HTML content to every visitor. Dynamic websites generate content on-the-fly based on user requests, database content, and server-side logic.

questions.question: Explain CSS box model.
questions.answer:
CSS Box Model:
The CSS Box Model is the fundamental layout concept in CSS. Every element on a web page is treated as a rectangular box with four layers:

1. Content Box: The innermost area where text and images appear. Size defined by width and height properties.

2. Padding: Transparent space between the content and the border. Adds space inside the element. Set with: padding, padding-top, padding-right, padding-bottom, padding-left.

3. Border: A line around the padding. Can have different styles (solid, dashed, dotted). Set with: border-width, border-style, border-color.

4. Margin: Transparent space outside the border. Separates the element from neighboring elements. Set with: margin, margin-top, margin-right, margin-bottom, margin-left.

Box Sizing Formula (default box-sizing: content-box):
Total Width = width + padding-left + padding-right + border-left + border-right
Total Height = height + padding-top + padding-bottom + border-top + border-bottom
(Margin is NOT included in element's own dimensions but affects layout spacing)

Diagram Layout (outer to inner):
[ Margin | Border | Padding | Content ]

Example: A div with width:200px, padding:15px, border:5px → total rendered width = 200+15+15+5+5 = 240px.

Tip: Use box-sizing: border-box to include padding and border in the width/height calculation.

Compare XML Schema with DTD.
questions.answer:
XML Schema (XSD) vs DTD:

| Feature              | DTD                                  | XML Schema (XSD)                        |
|----------------------|--------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------|
| Full Form            | Document Type Definition             | XML Schema Definition                   |
| Syntax               | Not XML syntax (own syntax)          | Written in XML syntax                   |
| Data Types           | Limited (PCDATA, CDATA only)         | Rich (string, integer, date, boolean, custom) |
| Namespace support    | No                                   | Yes, full namespace support             |
| Occurrence control   | ?, *, + (basic)                      | minOccurs, maxOccurs (precise control)  |
| Restrictions         | Cannot define value restrictions     | Can restrict values (min, max, pattern) |
| Reusability          | Limited reuse                        | Types can be defined and reused         |
| Extensibility        | Poor                                 | Supports inheritance and extension      |
| Readability          | Less readable                        | More verbose but readable as XML        |
| Complexity           | Simple for basic validation          | More complex but very powerful          |
| Default values       | Basic support                        | Full support for defaults/fixed values  |

Conclusion: DTD is simpler and older. XSD is more powerful, uses XML syntax, supports data types, namespaces, and complex restrictions. XSD is preferred for modern applications.
